note: Logic, quotes and structure check out; the E note correctly diagrams the contrapositive and the A note now teaches a repeatable move.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Most children under six are egocentric and selfish in their attitudes toward animals.

Ordinarily, children only begin to understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs somewhere between the ages of six and nine. So most children under six do not yet understand this.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Most children should not have pets until they are at least six years old.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Look at the conclusion's key word: "should." The evidence only describes what young children are like. The conclusion tells us what ought to happen. That "should not have pets" idea is a new concept in the conclusion, and on Sufficient Assumption the correct answer almost always has to supply it.

Let's argue with the psychologist. Given that most children under six don't yet understand that animals have their own feelings and needs, how could we argue that they should still have pets? Easy: maybe a child doesn't need to understand that to have a pet. A parent could do the caring, and the child could learn along the way. The argument never rules that out.

We can sketch it with arrows, as long as we remember the premise says "Ordinarily," so it is a "most" claim, not an "all" claim:

under 6 → not understand (most of them)
not understand → should not have pet (missing)

If every child who doesn't understand should not have a pet, then the "most" in the premise carries straight through: most children under six should not have pets.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We're looking for a rule that says children who don't understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs should not have pets:

not understand → should not have pet

The contrapositive is just as good: should have pet → understand. That version may be worded with only, so read the sentence carefully: after only if, the idea goes on the right side of the arrow, but in a sentence shaped like The only X are Y, the X goes on the left (X → Y). A rule linking "egocentric and selfish" to "should not have pets" would also work, because that premise is about the same group of children.

notes.body: A is about who takes care of the pet, and it never says what any child should or should not have. A sufficient assumption has to deliver the conclusion's new idea, "should not have pets." Combine A with the premises and you still can't say a word about what children should do.

Diagram it: understand → should be allowed to have pets. Our under-sixes mostly don't understand, so B's trigger never fires for them. B is the reversal of the rule we need (should have pets → understand). Knowing that children who understand may have pets says nothing about whether children who don't understand may have them too.

C says what is the case: most egocentric and selfish children "do not have pets." The conclusion is about what should be the case. A fact about who currently owns pets can't prove that anyone ought not to own one. No "should" goes in, so no "should" comes out.

D is tempting because it sounds like the premises, but that is the problem: it repeats the evidence (egocentric, doesn't understand) and adds nothing about what children should do. Stacking more evidence of the same kind never closes a gap to a "should" conclusion. Ask of every answer here: does it contain "should not have pets" or its contrapositive?

"The only children who should have pets are those who understand that their pets are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs." A sentence of the form The only X are Y means X → Y, so: should have pet → understand. Contrapositive: not understand → should not have pet.

Now chain it with the evidence. Most children under six → not understand → should not have pet. So most children under six should not have pets, which is the conclusion.

The move to repeat: find the new concept in the conclusion ("should not have pets"), then look for the rule that puts it on the right side of an arrow whose left side is something the evidence gives you.
